content.thinking:
I'm sketching out proportions for an African bush elephant—shoulder height around 3.2m, body length near 4.5m, tusks about 1.5-2m—and thinking through how to render it in a low-poly faceted style with flat colors.

Now I'm working out the skeleton layout in meters: body barrel height from belly (~1.0m) to back (~3.0m), width ~1.5m, with the rump and chest positioned along the z-axis to get the right overall length including head and trunk.

Then I'm placing the pelvis, spine chain, and chest/neck joints, followed by the head joint sized and positioned to sit above shoulder height with the forehead dome a bit higher, and finally the trunk root attaching at the front-bottom of the skull.

The trunk tapers from a 0.3m base radius down to 0.1m at the tip, hanging roughly 2.1m with a gentle forward curl near the end, so I'm laying out about six joints along that curve with a "tentacle" role. I'm also figuring out roles for the ears, deciding between "hinge" for flapping motion or possibly "fan".

Now I'm working out the leg structure, using pillar-like legs with shoulder, elbow, wrist, and foot joints positioned to keep the limbs mostly straight with slight bends, planning catmull paths and naming each joint in the chain accordingly.

For the feet I'm shaping a low-poly flattened cylinder base with toenails placed as small cone wedges in a ring at the front, and I'm tapering the leg radius from wider near the shoulder to narrower at the ankle. I'm also laying out the hind leg joints—hip, forward-bent knee, and hock—mirroring the front leg logic.

Now I'm setting up the body as a loft along a spine chain, defining the pelvis as the root joint and chaining the spine path from the rump through the back toward the neck base, so the body mesh can bend naturally along this skeletal structure.

Then I'm adding a short neck chain leading to the head joint, and a drooping tail chain rooted at the pelvis, hanging down and back with a tuft of coarse hair at the tip, positioning the base, mid, and droop points to give it a natural sag.

Still defining body stations...

Now I'm working through leg placement, making sure the legs attach inside the body with the outer radius extending slightly past the body's half-width so they read correctly. Then I move to the head, considering whether to build the skull as a swept shape or a simpler sphere/box hybrid for a low-poly look.

For the skull, I'm plotting out loft stations along the head's length — defining width, height, and position at each cross-section from the back of the dome down through the forehead toward where it meets the trunk, aiming for a tall domed elephant head shape roughly 1.3m from chin to crown.

I'm adding a separate lower jaw as a small tapered box positioned beneath the trunk root, with its own joint location, then defining the trunk itself as a wide flat-faced base tapering down to a narrow tip with two small finger-like protrusions, plus wrinkle rings painted along its length as texture stripes.

For the surface detail, I'm keeping the paint subtle to respect the flat-colour low-poly aesthetic -- darker banding on the trunk for wrinkles and a dusty gradient near the feet to suggest dust-bathing, rather than heavy texture work that would clash with the faceted style.

For the ears, I'm planning large Africa-shaped panels, roughly 1.2m tall and 1.1m wide, extruded with thin geometry and hinged at the rear of the head, tilted slightly outward to sit naturally against the skull.

Still defining ear geometry...

Checking that the ear position doesn't clip awkwardly into the shoulder or body width, and planning to give the ear interior a pink-gray tone with subtle vein detailing.

For the eyes, I'm placing small spheres on the side of the face near the forehead-trunk junction, with amber iris and dark pupil, plus eyelid wrinkles and a small temporal gland mark. Now I'm sizing the tusks appropriately for a bush elephant.

Checking tusk placement against the trunk to avoid overlap, then adding a small gum collar at the base. For the feet, I'm planning toenails (4 front, 3 hind for African elephants) as small low-poly shapes, and shaping the foot itself as a rounded cylinder or lathed profile tapering slightly at the ankle.

Placing nail wedges...

For skin color, I'm picking an African elephant palette: grayish-brown base with darker dorsal shading and a lighter belly, plus dusty tan on the lower legs, applied through flat color sectors for a low-poly faceted look.

Now I'm adding faceted body geometry with fewer sides for the low-poly style, and using band-based color sectors along the legs to create wrinkle details at knees and ankles plus a dustier tan tone toward the feet.

For the belly wrinkles, I'm thinking through how to position skin loops around the barrel in darker color, figuring out the right plane direction and lift so the loop encircles just the lower half without catching the legs.

Those flat belt-like folds could look off, so I'll shape them as lower-half arcs along the sides and belly plus neck folds, since elephant skin naturally creases that way. For texture, rather than flat untextured color, I'll use a subtle two-tone mottled paint blended with countershading and a dust gradient near the ground and legs—keeping low-poly facets but adding just enough variation to avoid looking unfinished.

I'm adding a cell-based crack pattern for wrinkled skin texture, darkening the lines where cell distances are close together to mimic elephant hide creases. Checking texel density at this scale—roughly 1024 texels over a 35m² body gives about 1cm resolution, which should be fine enough to render the crease detail convincingly.

I'm considering bumping paint resolution to 2048 for sharper wrinkle networks combined with mottling and a dust-gradient effect with a lighter belly, though that might strain the harness. All skin surfaces (body, legs, head, trunk, ears, tail) will share this base paint, with the trunk getting an extra ring pattern for its characteristic folds—spacing the rings every 7cm along its 2.2m length to get around 30 rings, darkening the underside slightly for a paler highlight on top.

For the head, I'm planning brow ridges, cheek bulges, domed forehead lobes, eyelid rings with small lash spikes around the eyes, a lower jaw with a subtle mouth line hidden beneath the trunk, and a nostril/finger detail at the trunk tip using small cone shapes with a dark disc for the nostril hole.

I'm also adding toenails, a coarse dark bristle tuft ringing the tail tip, sparse crown hairs on the head, chin whiskers, and two-toned tusks with a darker root band, worn chipped tips, and slight asymmetry — maybe the right tusk a touch shorter and chipped for realism.

Now I'm layering dust patches onto the back using tan noise so the whole upper surface looks dust-bathed, then coloring the ears with mottled pinkish-grey and darker vein lines plus darker rim edges, and setting flat base colors for the amber eyes, dark pupils, nails, and tusks.

Next I'm sketching out the rig: pelvis, spine chain, neck, head, jaw, a multi-segment trunk, ear hinges, rigid tusks, and full leg chains for both front and hind limbs plus a tail, totaling around 35 joints, with hind legs parenting off the pelvis and front legs off the chest joint.

Now for the tail, I need it to branch off the hips near where the rump ends around z=-1.9 to -1.95, parented to the hips joint.

For the body loft, I'll limit the bone influence to the spine chain plus hips, letting stations up to around z=1.25-1.3 cover the chest, and leave the neck and head as separate skinned pieces -- the head loft starts around z=1.0 to overlap slightly with the body front so there's no visible gap, and since the head attaches near the shoulders directly, this overlap should look natural even as the head rotates.

Now I'm working out the leg skinning: each leg is a smooth tapered sweep from shoulder/hip joint down to the foot, with front legs tapering from about 0.34 at the top to 0.28 mid to 0.24 at the ankle, and hind legs starting thicker at 0.38 for the thigh. The feet are separate flat cylinders attached at the leg tips, tapering slightly from top to bottom radius, and I'm positioning the ground plane just barely below zero so the feet appear to sink in slightly for contact.

I'm placing claws—four on the front feet, three on the hind, matching elephant anatomy—and working out the full joint hierarchy for both hind and front legs, tracing hip to knee to hock to foot and shoulder to elbow to wrist, adjusting each joint's x/y/z coordinates so the limbs bend naturally with the knee forward and the lower leg angling back toward the foot.

Now I'm checking proportions: narrowing the leg spacing to 0.52 on the x-axis so the legs sit properly under the 1.5-wide body, bumping overall height toward a bull elephant's scale around 3.3 meters, and starting to lay out the trunk's path from the skull base downward with a tapering radius.

I'm plotting the trunk curve point by point, aiming for a gentle S-shape that lifts slightly at the tip rather than dragging on the ground, and estimating the total trunk length by summing the segment distances as I go.

I'm setting up the trunk as a 7-segment tentacle chain tapering from 0.30 down to 0.075, rooted inside the skull and blending into the face near the front of the head.

For the jaw, I'm lofting a small lower jaw shape that tapers from the base near the trunk toward the front, with a jaw joint and bone, plus a hanging lower lip in a lighter pinkish tone and subtle mouth corners.

Now I'm adding tusk collars and cheek bulges as flattened low-poly spheres on either side of the skull, then working out eye placement on the head's surface—using a surface-projection approach to stick the eyes onto the skull near the upper front sides rather than guessing coordinates directly.

For the eye detail itself, I'm layering a dark wrinkled socket ring, an amber eyeball, a darker pupil, a small lid arc, and a ring of lash spikes above. Then I'm moving to the forehead, placing two domed lobes on the crown to mimic the bi-lobed shape elephants have there.

Ear joints attach to the head at a fixed offset, and I'm clarifying the coordinate convention so left/right suffixes map correctly to world-space X rather than local model space. With the geometry mapped out, I'm ready to write the actual code using the paint helper functions for ribs and rings.

Writing skin color palette and crease noise function...

Still writing skin paint logic...

Blending the ring groove effect into the base skin paint, letting the gradient darken toward grooves while keeping recursive paint resolution intact. For the tusk, I'm sweeping a tapered profile along catmull points with shrinking radii toward the tip, coloring it with ivory bands that darken slightly near the root and tip.

Writing tusk path coordinates...

For the right tusk, I'll make it slightly shorter and chipped-looking by truncating the path and giving it a flatter end cap to suggest damage. Then I'll add toe nails as small box shapes arranged in a ring around the front of each foot near ground level.

Positioning nails using outward angles per foot, oriented with their outward axis matching the direction away from the foot center, tilted up slightly so they look natural against the ground. The nails attach to the final tip joint of each leg's bone chain.

Naming the chain joints per leg -- front legs as shoulder/elbow/wrist/foot, hind legs as hip/knee/hock/foot -- and treating the sweep path along each chain so it spans from the top joint to the foot tip. Making sure the foot cylinder's cap sits just inside the leg's rounded end so there's no visible gap between the leg sweep and the foot geometry.

Now I'm working out the tail chain parented to the hips, placing a short sequence of tapering points from the rump outward with shrinking radius toward the tip, then adding a tuft of ring spikes at the very end using the last chain point's frame.

Writing tuft spikes...

I'm also planning smaller scatter-based hair bristles across the crown of the skull, filtering for upward-facing normals above a certain height so they only appear on top.

Now I'm setting up ear hinge joints attaching to the head with appropriate position and direction, then thinking through optional surface details like belly folds, hip bumps, shoulder blades, and a spine ridge, deciding most of these are too subtle to bother with except for sparse hair cards on the forehead and back using the same spike technique.

Rather than individual stick parts for the bristle hairs (which would blow the part budget), I'm switching to cards with a small hair texture so a whole tuft becomes a single part—using this approach for the crown, back ridge, chin, and ear edges while keeping spikes for the tail tuft since that's a smaller set. I'm also considering sweeping a few geometric loops for belly girth folds and neck folds, each as its own part.

For the leg wrinkles, rather than separate band geometry, I'll bake knee-crease rings directly into the leg's procedural paint—darkening thin horizontal bands at the knee height using a noise-modulated sine pattern on the y-coordinate, applied only below the knee zone.

For feet, I'll reuse the skin paint with a darker sole tone and the same dust-darkening at low y values. I'm skipping an explicit mouth line and instead relying on the jaw/chin geometry with a lower lip hint. For hair cards, I'm sketching a small SVG bristle tuft with three curved dark strokes scaled to fit a 128px texture, then scattering sparse coarse hairs across the back using a surface-normal filter so most are hidden except where the normal points upward.

I'm also planning tufts at the crown, chin, and ear rim, plus a few forehead wrinkle arcs drawn as draped sweeps across the brow using Catmull-Rom curves projected onto the skull surface. A small dark temple gland streak gets added too, while I'm skipping extras like a shoulder bump, belly, or genitalia, and just adding a subtle lower lip bulge. I'm now tallying up the part count: body, head loft, cheeks, lobes, ears, and eye socs so far.

Rounding out the estimate, I count toward roughly 90 parts total once tusks, collars, trunk tip details, legs, feet, nails, tail tuft, jaw, folds, brow arcs, and detail cards are all included. I'm also considering adding finer touches like ear veins and thicker rimmed edges painted via normal-based thickness, then moving into coding the actual loft and sweep calls with bone chains and joints, using faceted (non-smooth) shading on an 8-sided body loft for a low-poly look.

Working through the ear geometry next—setting side counts (10 for body, 8 for head), defining the jaw bone role, and using flattened spheres for cheeks and forehead. I'm figuring out the ear's extrusion outline direction using cross products to get the correct outward thickness vector for left versus right ears, then placing the outline points so the ear hangs naturally from its attachment point at the front-top edge near the head, with the root edge running vertically down the side of the skull.

Now I'm finalizing the ear's outline coordinates point by point, then checking the overall proportions against a reference African ear size at this creature's shoulder height, confirming the ear's attachment position puts its lowest point, backward extent, and outward extent all in reasonable positions relative to the body's width so it flares out properly without clipping into the torso.

I'm noticing the ear slab overlaps slightly with the front leg geometry near the lower section, so I'm adjusting the ear's rotation and flare angle outward to reduce that intersection.

Actually flipping the tilt direction so the ear's bottom points outward instead of inward, then moving on to write the actual code — starting with the torso loft and a surface helper for the fold details.

Now I'm working out the head loft stations, bone, and neck-fill geometry so the head blends smoothly into the body, then roughing in the jaw joint with its own loft stations and skin coloring before setting up eye placement.

Placing eyes using the nearest surface point on the skull loft, oriented by the hit normal, then layering a small amber eye sphere, a flattened darker lid-ring socket, and a tiny pupil offset from the hit point to finish the eye detail.

Adding spiky lash details to the eye ring. Now I'm ready to write the file, double-checking that paint utilities like noise, cells, mix, smoothstep, resolve, and rgb are all properly exported before moving on to defining the trunk length.

Checking the body sweep configuration — the bone list combines the spine chain with the hips joint, which handles the tail attachment and rump region correctly since the spine path originates from the hips position.

I'm realizing there's a degenerate bone issue if the hips joint's child spine1 sits at the same position — zero-length bone. I need to offset the hips root slightly so the bone between hips and spine1 spans a real distance, rather than collapsing to a point.

Settling on hips at (0,2.5,-1.6) with spine1 at (0,2.5,-1.2), giving a 0.4m bone, then continuing the spine chain through spine2 and spine3 up to the neck and head joints, with neck parented to spine3. Now I'm working out how the front legs should parent off this same hierarchy.
